title: Titanic: The Final 2 Hours and 40 Minutes
alt_titles: How the Titanic Really Sank, Minute by Minute
Titanic: The Night the Unsinkable Ship Went Down
The Titanic Disaster: Warnings, Lifeboats and the Ship That Didn't Come
description_summary: Just before midnight on 14 April 1912, the largest ship afloat struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic. This is the story of the two hours and forty minutes that followed: the ignored warnings, the half-empty lifeboats, the ship that saw the rockets, the rescue, and how the disaster changed safety at sea.

scenes.narration: At twenty to midnight on Sunday the fourteenth of April, 1912, lookout Frederick Fleet saw a dark shape ahead in the North Atlantic. He rang three warning bells and telephoned the bridge of the Titanic, the largest ship afloat. His message was simple. Iceberg, right ahead. Less than a minute later, the ship struck it.

shots.caption: Frederick Fleet, the lookout who saw the iceberg
An iceberg photographed near the site in April 1912
Titanic's crow's nest, high on the foremast

scenes.narration: Two hours and forty minutes later, Titanic was gone. More than fifteen hundred people died, most of them in water just below freezing. About seven hundred survived, the majority of them women and children. They escaped in lifeboats that had been lowered with hundreds of seats left empty. Help was on its way, but it was hours too far away.

shots.file: File:Photograph of a Lifeboat Carrying Titanic Survivors - NARA - 278337.jpg
shots.caption: A lifeboat carrying Titanic survivors, 15 April 1912

scenes.narration: This is the story of those two hours and forty minutes. It begins with the warnings that went unheeded. It includes a ship close enough to see Titanic's rockets, and a rescue that came too late for most. And it ends with how the disaster changed safety at sea for good.

shots.caption: Titanic's planned route, and where she sank
The SS Californian

shots.file: File:Color postcard of R. M. S Carpathia, ca. 1912.jpg
shots.caption: The Carpathia, on a postcard from around 1912

scenes.narration: Titanic was built at the Harland and Wolff shipyard in Belfast for the White Star Line. She was launched in May 1911, beside her near identical sister ship, Olympic. At almost eight hundred and eighty three feet long, she was the largest ship in the world when she entered service.

shots.file: File:Arrol Gantry with Liners Olympic & Titanic in Construction.jpg
shots.query: Olympic and Titanic under construction Belfast
shots.caption: Olympic and Titanic under construction in Belfast
Titanic ready for launch, Belfast, May 1911
Titanic and her sister ship Olympic in Belfast

scenes.narration: She was built for comfort as much as speed. First class passengers had a grand staircase, a gymnasium, a swimming pool and Turkish baths. The best suites cost a fortune. In 1911, the trade journal The Shipbuilder described the new White Star liners as practically unsinkable.

shots.file: File:Drawing of the Grand Staircase onboard the RMS Titanic from the 1912 promotional booklet.jpg
shots.caption: The Grand Staircase, from a 1912 promotional booklet
A White Star Line advertisement, April 1912

scenes.narration: Her hull was divided into sixteen compartments, separated by watertight bulkheads. She could stay afloat with up to four of the forward ones flooded. But she carried just twenty lifeboats, with room for 1,178 people. That was more than British rules demanded. Those rules had simply not kept pace with the size of new ships.

shots.caption: Thomas Andrews of the Harland and Wolff shipyard

shots.file: File:Titanic starboard bow by Father Browne.jpg
shots.caption: Titanic's bow, photographed by Father Browne, April 1912

scenes.narration: On Wednesday the tenth of April 1912, Titanic left Southampton on her maiden voyage to New York. She called at Cherbourg in France that evening, and at Queenstown in Ireland the next day. Then she turned west into the open Atlantic, with about 2,200 passengers and crew on board.

shots.caption: Titanic leaves Southampton, 10 April 1912
One of the last photos of Titanic, off Ireland, 11 April 1912
Titanic at the start of her maiden voyage, April 1912

scenes.narration: Sunday the fourteenth of April began quietly. But through the day, Titanic's wireless operators received a series of messages from other ships. Six of them warned of ice ahead. Some were passed to Captain Edward Smith, a veteran with decades at sea. Others never reached the bridge at all.

shots.caption: Captain Edward Smith
The wireless room of Titanic's sister ship, Olympic

scenes.narration: The two wireless operators, Jack Phillips and Harold Bride, worked for the Marconi company, not the White Star Line. Their main job was sending passengers' private messages. That evening they were busy with a backlog of them, relayed through a station at Cape Race in Newfoundland.

shots.caption: Jack Phillips, Titanic's senior wireless operator
The wireless station at Cape Race, Newfoundland

scenes.narration: The night was clear, calm and moonless. With no swell, there were no waves breaking white around the base of an iceberg to give it away. Titanic kept up a speed of about twenty two knots. High in the crow's nest, Fleet and fellow lookout Reginald Lee had no binoculars.

shots.file: File:Possible Titanic iceberg from SS Birma.jpg
shots.caption: An iceberg seen from the ship Birma near the site, 1912

card.label: Titanic's speed at the time of the collision

shots.file: File:Captain Smith and the officers of the RMS Titanic in 1912.jpg
shots.caption: Captain Smith with ship's officers, 1912

scenes.narration: Not far away, a smaller ship called the Californian had stopped for the night, surrounded by ice. Its wireless operator, Cyril Evans, had tried to warn Titanic about the ice earlier that evening. At half past eleven, with no orders to stay on duty, he switched off his set and went to bed.

shots.query: SS Californian wireless operator Cyril Evans
shots.caption: Cyril Evans, the Californian's wireless operator
Ships in the area on the night of the sinking

scenes.narration: Ten minutes later, Fleet saw the iceberg. On the bridge, First Officer William Murdoch ordered the ship turned hard and the engines reversed. Titanic began to swing, but too slowly. The iceberg scraped along her starboard side below the waterline, buckling plates and popping rivets.

shots.query: William Murdoch Titanic first officer portrait
shots.caption: First Officer William Murdoch
The collision, as shown in a 1912 illustration

scenes.narration: Many passengers felt only a slight shudder and a grinding noise. Some went back to bed. On the forward deck, a few people even played with chunks of ice that had fallen onto the ship. Below, sea water was already pouring into the forward compartments.

shots.query: Titanic passengers on deck April 1912 photograph
shots.caption: Passengers on Titanic's deck, April 1912
Titanic's promenade deck

scenes.narration: Captain Smith inspected the damage with Thomas Andrews, the shipyard's chief naval architect, who was on board for the maiden voyage. Six compartments were open to the sea. That was more than the ship could survive. Andrews told the captain that Titanic would sink, perhaps within an hour or two.

shots.caption: Titanic's watertight compartments

scenes.narration: Just after midnight, Smith ordered the lifeboats uncovered and distress calls sent. Phillips and Bride tapped out the old distress code, CQD, and later the newer signal, SOS. Several ships heard them. The nearest to respond was the Cunard liner Carpathia, fifty eight miles away.

shots.caption: A wireless message from the night of the sinking

shots.query: Harold Bride Titanic wireless operator portrait
shots.caption: Harold Bride, Titanic's junior wireless operator

scenes.narration: The Carpathia's captain, Arthur Rostron, turned his ship around at once. He cut the heating and hot water so that every ounce of steam went to the engines. He posted extra lookouts for ice, and had doctors, blankets and ladders made ready for survivors.

shots.file: File:Captain arthur henry rostron of carpathia.jpg
shots.caption: Captain Arthur Rostron of the Carpathia

shots.query: RMS Carpathia ship at sea photograph
shots.caption: The Carpathia at sea

scenes.narration: On Titanic, the first lifeboat, number seven, was lowered at about quarter to one. It could hold sixty five people. It left with about twenty eight. At first, many passengers did not believe the great ship was in danger. A cold lifeboat on a dark ocean seemed the greater risk.

card.label: People in the first lifeboat lowered

shots.caption: Titanic's boat deck and lifeboats

scenes.narration: The officers followed the rule of women and children first. On one side of the ship, men were sometimes allowed in when no women were waiting. On the other side, they were mostly kept out. From around twenty past one, the crew fired white distress rockets into the night sky.

shots.query: women and children first Titanic lifeboats illustration
shots.caption: Loading the lifeboats, from a 1912 illustration

scenes.narration: On the Californian, officers on watch saw a large ship to the south, and then white rockets above her. They reported them to Captain Stanley Lord. No one woke the wireless operator, and the Californian stayed where she was. How far away she really was, and what Lord understood, is still argued over today.

shots.caption: Captain Stanley Lord of the Californian

scenes.narration: As the bow sank deeper, the loading grew more desperate. White Star chairman Bruce Ismay stepped into a collapsible boat at about twenty to two. He survived, and was condemned for it for the rest of his life. The last boat to be lowered left at five past two.

shots.file: File:J. Bruce Ismay, White Star Line Manager.jpg
shots.caption: J. Bruce Ismay, chairman of the White Star Line
Titanic's last lifeboat, photographed from the Carpathia

scenes.narration: The ship's band played on deck to keep the passengers calm. It is often said that their last tune was the hymn Nearer, My God, to Thee. Survivors disagreed, and some remembered ragtime instead. No one knows for certain what was played at the end. None of the musicians survived.

shots.caption: Bandleader Wallace Hartley and the ship's musicians

card.text: A hymn, or ragtime? Survivors disagreed

scenes.narration: At around quarter past two, the bow plunged under and the stern rose high into the air. The lights flickered and went out. Then the hull tore apart between the funnels. At twenty past two in the morning, Titanic disappeared beneath the Atlantic.

shots.caption: The sinking as imagined by Willy Stöwer, 1912
The final moments, as later illustrated

scenes.narration: More than a thousand people were left in the water. It was about minus two degrees Celsius, and most died of the cold within minutes. Only a few boats went back. Fifth Officer Harold Lowe returned in lifeboat fourteen and pulled four people from the sea. One of them later died.

shots.query: Harold Lowe Titanic fifth officer portrait
shots.caption: Fifth Officer Harold Lowe

scenes.narration: The Carpathia arrived at about four in the morning, an hour and a half after Titanic sank. As dawn broke, her crew could see icebergs all around them, and lifeboats scattered across miles of sea. Over the next four and a half hours, they took the survivors aboard. In total, about seven hundred and ten people were saved.

shots.caption: Titanic's lifeboats, brought to New York by the Carpathia
Survivors aboard the Carpathia

scenes.narration: Who survived depended heavily on class. According to the British inquiry, around sixty two per cent of first class passengers were saved. In third class it was only about one in four, and among the crew slightly fewer. Nearly three quarters of the women on board survived, but only about one man in five.

chart.title: Share of people saved, by class

scenes.narration: The Carpathia reached New York on the evening of Thursday the eighteenth of April, in heavy rain. Huge crowds were waiting at the pier. By then, newspapers around the world had carried the news. Harold Bride, his feet badly injured, had to be carried ashore.

shots.file: File:19120415 New Liner Titanic Hits an Iceberg - The New York Times.png
shots.caption: The New York Times, 15 April 1912
A London newspaper seller with news of the disaster

shots.file: File:Harold Bride, surviving wireless operator of the TITANIC, with feet bandaged, being carried up ramp of ship LCCN2002714434.jpg
shots.query: Harold Bride carried ashore New York
shots.caption: Harold Bride, injured, is carried ashore in New York

scenes.narration: Inquiries were held in both the United States and Britain. They found that Titanic had been going too fast for the ice conditions. They also found that the lifeboat rules were badly out of date. The Californian's captain was heavily criticised for failing to respond to the rockets.

shots.caption: The United States Senate inquiry, 1912

shots.file: File:J. Bruce Ismay being questioned by Senate Investigating Committee.jpg
shots.caption: Bruce Ismay questioned by the Senate inquiry

shots.query: Lord Mersey British Wreck Commissioner Titanic inquiry
shots.caption: The British inquiry, led by Lord Mersey

scenes.narration: The changes that followed still shape safety at sea. In 1914, a new international convention required lifeboat places for everyone on board, and regular drills. Passenger ships had to keep a radio watch twenty four hours a day. An International Ice Patrol was set up to track icebergs in the North Atlantic.

shots.query: International Ice Patrol Coast Guard iceberg aircraft
shots.caption: The International Ice Patrol, set up in 1914

card.text: The first Safety of Life at Sea convention

scenes.narration: For seventy three years, the wreck lay undiscovered. Many expeditions searched for it and failed. Then, on the first of September 1985, a French and American team led by Jean-Louis Michel and Robert Ballard found it. It lay about three thousand eight hundred metres down, south of Newfoundland.

shots.caption: Oceanographer Robert Ballard

shots.file: File:RMS Titanic wreck depth to scale.jpg
shots.caption: How deep the wreck lies, shown to scale

scenes.narration: The wreck settled one of the oldest arguments about the sinking. Several survivors had said the ship broke in two, but the official inquiries had doubted them. On the seabed, the bow and stern lie about six hundred metres apart. The survivors had been right all along. Today, bacteria are slowly eating away at the steel, and the wreck is gradually collapsing.

shots.caption: The bow of the wreck on the seabed
The stern section of the wreck

scenes.narration: Titanic was not sunk by a single mistake. Ice warnings, speed, missing binoculars, too few lifeboats and a silent radio all played a part. Every passenger ship since has sailed under rules written because of that night. Sources and image credits are in the description.
